text: Article 2 of DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) defines the scope of the Regulation. Article 2(1) states that the Regulation applies to a broad range of financial entities, beginning with: (a) credit institutions; (b) payment institutions and account information service providers; (c) electronic money institutions; (d) investment firms — and continuing with further categories such as central counterparties, trading venues, insurance and reinsurance undertakings, and ICT third-party service providers. DORA therefore applies to credit institutions of every business model: retail banks such as Crédit Aurore are credit institutions and are fully in scope, alongside investment banks. The Regulation is not limited to large investment banks, and there is no exemption for retail or deposit-taking banks. Article 4 establishes a proportionality principle: the ICT risk-management requirements are implemented taking into account the entity's size, overall risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of its services — proportionality adjusts the depth of the measures, it does not remove retail banks from the scope of the Regulation.

Article 5 of the Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), titled Governance and organisation, requires financial entities to have in place an internal governance and control framework that ensures an effective and prudent management of ICT risk in order to achieve a high level of digital operational resilience. The management body of the financial entity bears the ultimate responsibility for managing ICT risk and cannot delegate it away. Specifically, the management body must define, approve, oversee and be accountable for the implementation of all arrangements related to the ICT risk management framework. It must put in place policies aimed at ensuring high standards of availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data, set clear roles and responsibilities for all ICT-related functions, and establish appropriate governance arrangements ensuring effective and timely communication, cooperation and coordination among those functions. The management body must approve and periodically review the ICT business continuity policy and response and recovery plans, approve and review the internal ICT audit plans, allocate and periodically review an appropriate budget to fulfil the entity's digital operational resilience needs, and approve the policy on the use of ICT services provided by third-party providers. Members of the management body must actively keep up to date with sufficient knowledge and skills to understand and assess ICT risk and its impact, including by following specific training on a regular basis. The governance framework must be documented and reviewed at least once a year.

Article 6 of DORA sets out the requirements for the ICT risk management framework. Financial entities must have a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework as part of their overall risk management system, which enables them to address ICT risk quickly, efficiently and comprehensively and to ensure a high level of digital operational resilience. The framework must include the strategies, policies, procedures, ICT protocols and tools necessary to duly and adequately protect all information assets and ICT assets, including computer software, hardware and servers, as well as relevant physical components and infrastructures. Financial entities must minimise the impact of ICT risk by deploying appropriate strategies, policies, procedures, protocols and tools. They must map and keep updated the configuration of their information and ICT assets and the dependencies between them. The framework must be documented and reviewed at least once a year, and upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents, as well as following supervisory instructions or conclusions derived from relevant digital operational resilience testing or audit processes. It must be subject to internal audit by auditors on a regular basis in line with the entity's audit plan, and auditors must possess sufficient knowledge, skills and expertise in ICT risk. Financial entities must assign responsibility for managing and overseeing ICT risk to a control function and ensure an appropriate level of independence of that control function to avoid conflicts of interest. The framework must include a digital operational resilience strategy setting out how it is implemented.

text: Article 10 of DORA, titled Detection, requires financial entities to have in place mechanisms to promptly detect anomalous activities, in accordance with Article 17, including ICT network performance issues and ICT-related incidents, and to identify potential material single points of failure. All detection mechanisms must be regularly tested in accordance with the testing provisions of the Regulation. The detection mechanisms must enable multiple layers of control, define alert thresholds and criteria to trigger and initiate ICT-related incident response processes, including automatic alert mechanisms for relevant staff in charge of ICT-related incident response. Financial entities must devote sufficient resources and capabilities to monitor user activity, the occurrence of ICT anomalies and ICT-related incidents, in particular cyber-attacks. For financial entities that are not microenterprises, the detection capability must allow the collection and analysis of information from internal and, where relevant, external sources to identify anomalies in a timely manner. Effective detection is a cornerstone of operational resilience because the speed at which an anomaly or intrusion is identified directly determines the scope for containment and recovery. For an AI-driven banking support agent, detection includes monitoring for abnormal query patterns, prompt-injection attempts, data exfiltration signals and unexpected tool invocations, with alerting tied into the incident response process. The mechanisms must be designed to reduce false negatives while keeping false positives manageable, and must be calibrated and tested as part of the resilience programme.

text: Article 17 of DORA establishes the ICT-related incident management process. Financial entities must define, establish and implement an ICT-related incident management process to detect, manage and notify ICT-related incidents. They must record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats, and must establish appropriate procedures and processes to ensure a consistent and integrated monitoring, handling and follow-up of ICT-related incidents, so as to ensure that root causes are identified, documented and addressed in order to prevent the occurrence of such incidents. The incident management process must set up early-warning indicators; establish procedures to identify, track, log, categorise and classify ICT-related incidents according to their priority and severity and according to the criticality of the services impacted; assign roles and responsibilities that need to be activated for different incident types and scenarios; set out plans for communication to staff, external stakeholders and media, and for notification to clients, for internal escalation procedures, including ICT-related customer complaints, as well as for the provision of information to financial entities acting as counterparts, as appropriate. Financial entities must ensure that at least major ICT-related incidents are reported to relevant senior management and inform the management body of major incidents, explaining the impact, response and additional controls to be established. The classification of incidents under Article 18 feeds directly into the reporting obligations under Article 19, making a robust internal taxonomy essential.

text: Article 19 of DORA governs the reporting of major ICT-related incidents and, on a voluntary basis, significant cyber threats to the relevant competent authority. Financial entities must report major ICT-related incidents to the competent authority within the time limits laid down in the regulatory and implementing technical standards. The reporting follows a staged approach comprising an initial notification, an intermediate report when the status of the original incident has changed significantly or the handling has changed based on new information, and a final report when the root cause analysis has been completed, regardless of whether mitigation measures have already been implemented, and when the actual impact figures are available to replace estimates. The technical standards specify the content and the binding time limits (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301): the initial notification is due as early as possible and in any case within four hours of classifying the incident as major, and no later than 24 hours from the moment the financial entity became aware of it; the intermediate report is due at the latest within 72 hours from the submission of the initial notification, even where the status of the incident has not changed; and the final report is due no later than one month after the submission of the intermediate report or its latest update. Reporting a major ICT-related incident is therefore never left to the entity's discretion: binding deadlines apply from the moment of classification. Financial entities may outsource the reporting obligations to a third-party provider but remain fully responsible for the fulfilment of those obligations. Where a major incident has or may have an impact on the financial interests of clients, the financial entity must, without undue delay, inform its clients about the incident and about the measures taken to mitigate the adverse effects. Competent authorities provide details to other relevant authorities, including the European Supervisory Authorities and, where relevant, the European Central Bank and national authorities. The harmonised reporting reduces fragmentation across the single market.

text: Article 26 of DORA introduces advanced testing of ICT tools, systems and processes based on threat-led penetration testing (TLPT). Financial entities identified by competent authorities as significant, taking into account their size, risk profile and systemic importance, must carry out at least every three years advanced testing by means of TLPT. TLPT is a controlled attempt to compromise the critical functions of a financial entity by simulating the tactics, techniques and procedures of real-life threat actors, conducted on live production systems. Each TLPT must cover several or all of the critical or important functions of the entity and must be performed on the live systems supporting such functions. Financial entities must identify all relevant underlying ICT systems, processes and technologies supporting critical or important functions, including those supported through ICT third-party service providers, and the scope must be validated by the competent authority or its designated TLPT authority. The testing methodology in the European Union follows the TIBER-EU framework. Testers must meet requirements as to suitability, reputation, competence and independence, and where internal testers are used the entity must also engage external testers at least every third test. At the conclusion of the test, the entity provides the authorities with the relevant documentation confirming that the test was conducted in accordance with the requirements, and receives an attestation. Mutual recognition of TLPT results across Member States avoids duplicative testing for entities operating cross-border.

Article 28 of DORA sets out the general principles for the sound management of ICT third-party risk. Financial entities must manage ICT third-party risk as an integral component of ICT risk within their ICT risk management framework, and in accordance with the principle of full responsibility for compliance with all obligations under the Regulation and applicable financial services law, which remains with the financial entity even where it relies on ICT third-party service providers. Financial entities may only enter into contractual arrangements with ICT third-party service providers that comply with appropriate information security standards. They must maintain and update a register of information in relation to all contractual arrangements on the use of ICT services provided by third-party providers, distinguishing between those supporting critical or important functions and others, and report at least yearly to competent authorities on the number of new arrangements, the categories of providers, the types of services and the functions supported. Before entering into a contractual arrangement, the financial entity must assess whether the arrangement covers a critical or important function, assess supervisory conditions, identify and assess all relevant risks including concentration risk, and undertake due diligence on prospective providers. Article 28 also requires entities to ensure that contracts can be terminated in defined circumstances, such as a significant breach by the provider, and to have exit strategies and transition plans in place for ICT services supporting critical or important functions, so that the entity can exit without disruption to its business and without detriment to compliance.

text: Article 30 of DORA specifies the key contractual provisions that must be included in the arrangements between financial entities and ICT third-party service providers. For all ICT services, the contract must set out a clear and complete description of all functions and services, including whether subcontracting of ICT services supporting a critical or important function is permitted and under which conditions; the locations where the contracted or subcontracted services are to be provided and where data is to be processed; provisions on availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality in relation to the protection of data; provisions on ensuring access, recovery and return of data in case of insolvency, resolution, discontinuation of business operations of the provider, or termination of the contract; service level descriptions; the obligation of the provider to assist at no additional cost, or at a pre-determined cost, when an ICT incident related to the service occurs; the obligation to fully cooperate with the competent authorities; and termination rights and minimum notice periods. For arrangements supporting critical or important functions, additional provisions are required, including full service level descriptions with precise quantitative and qualitative performance targets, notice periods and reporting obligations of the provider, requirements to implement and test business contingency plans and ICT security measures, participation in the financial entity's threat-led penetration testing where relevant, monitoring rights including unrestricted rights of access, inspection and audit by the entity, the authorities and appointed third parties, and exit strategies with a mandatory adequate transition period. The European Supervisory Authorities develop standard contractual clauses to support compliance.

Article 45 of DORA addresses information-sharing arrangements on cyber threat information and intelligence. Financial entities may exchange among themselves cyber threat information and intelligence, including indicators of compromise, tactics, techniques and procedures, cyber security alerts and configuration tools, to the extent that such information sharing aims to enhance the digital operational resilience of financial entities, takes place within trusted communities of financial entities, and is implemented through information-sharing arrangements that protect the potentially sensitive nature of the information shared and that are governed by rules of conduct in full respect of business confidentiality, the protection of personal data in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation, and competition policy. The objective of the article is to strengthen collective defence by enabling the timely dissemination of actionable threat intelligence, so that an attack observed by one entity can be anticipated and mitigated by others before it spreads across the sector. Such arrangements must define the conditions for participation and, where relevant, the involvement of public authorities and ICT third-party service providers. Financial entities must notify the competent authorities of their participation in such information-sharing arrangements upon validation of their membership, or of the cessation of their membership once it takes effect. Information sharing under Article 45 is voluntary, but it is encouraged as an effective tool because cyber threats rarely target a single institution in isolation, and shared intelligence raises the resilience of the financial ecosystem as a whole while respecting legal safeguards.

text: Recital 3 of DORA explains the context and objectives that motivated the Regulation. It recognises that ICT risk poses challenges to the operational resilience, performance and stability of the Union financial system, and that, despite efforts at national and Union level, ICT risk had not been addressed in a consistent manner, with rules that were either incomplete or overlapping, sometimes contradictory and frequently fragmented across sectors and Member States. The recital notes that prior Union financial services legislation had addressed ICT risk only indirectly, as part of broader operational risk requirements, and that the resulting patchwork left gaps and created regulatory arbitrage and compliance burdens for entities operating cross-border. DORA was therefore conceived to consolidate and upgrade ICT risk requirements into a single, coherent and comprehensive framework applicable across the financial sector, covering credit institutions, payment institutions, investment firms, insurance undertakings, crypto-asset service providers and many other categories of financial entity, as well as introducing an oversight framework for critical ICT third-party service providers. The overarching aim is to ensure that all participants in the financial system are subject to a common set of standards to mitigate ICT risk, so that the sector can withstand, respond to and recover from ICT-related disruptions and threats, thereby preserving financial stability and consumer protection and supporting the smooth functioning of the internal market in an increasingly digitalised environment. The recital frames the proportionate application of the rules according to the size and risk profile of entities.

DORA mandates the European Supervisory Authorities, through the Joint Committee, to develop regulatory technical standards (RTS) and implementing technical standards (ITS) that operationalise the incident classification and reporting regime under Articles 18 and 19. The RTS on the classification of ICT-related incidents specify the criteria for determining whether an incident is major, the materiality thresholds for each criterion, and the criteria and thresholds for identifying significant cyber threats. The classification criteria include the number and relevance of clients, financial counterparts and transactions affected; the reputational impact; the duration and service downtime of the incident; the geographical spread in terms of areas affected; the data losses in relation to availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality of data; the criticality of the services affected, including the entity's critical or important functions; and the economic impact in absolute and relative terms, covering direct and indirect costs and losses. An incident is generally classified as major when it meets a defined combination of these criteria above the specified thresholds. The ITS standardise the reporting templates and the forms, formats and procedures financial entities must use to report major incidents and notify significant cyber threats, ensuring consistency of the information transmitted to competent authorities across the Union. Together, the RTS and ITS provide the granular, harmonised methodology that turns the high-level obligations of the Regulation into a workable and comparable reporting process, reducing divergence between Member States and supporting aggregated supervisory analysis of operational risk in the sector.

text: DORA was adopted as Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector, and was published in the Official Journal of the European Union in December 2022. It entered into force on the twentieth day following its publication, on 16 January 2023, but provided for a transitional implementation period of twenty-four months before becoming applicable. As a result, DORA applies from 17 January 2025, the date from which financial entities and, where relevant, their ICT third-party service providers must comply with its requirements. Because DORA is a regulation rather than a directive, it is directly applicable in all Member States without the need for national transposition, although it is accompanied by the directive amending several existing sectoral directives to ensure consistency. The substantive obligations are detailed in a set of regulatory and implementing technical standards developed by the European Supervisory Authorities, delivered in two batches with the first set of standards finalised during 2024 in time for the application date and a second batch following. National competent authorities such as BaFin in Germany and the ACPR and AMF in France supervise compliance within their respective mandates, while a new oversight framework, led by lead overseers designated among the European Supervisory Authorities, applies to ICT third-party service providers designated as critical. Financial entities were expected to have their ICT risk management frameworks, incident reporting processes, resilience testing programmes and third-party registers in place by the application date.
